paragraphs: Graph coarsening replaces a large graph with a smaller one so that graph computations become easier. The challenge is deciding what the smaller graph should preserve. This paper studies preservation of distances between graphs, bringing a geometric perspective to methods that aim to retain spectral information.

The authors treat graphs as points in a space whose distances are measured using the Gromov–Wasserstein distance. They bound how much the distance between two graphs can change when both are coarsened. This makes the relationship between different graphs an explicit target of compression, which matters when learning from an entire collection of graphs.

The resulting discrepancy can be minimized using weighted kernel K-means. With an appropriate kernel, this approach improves existing spectrum-preserving methods. Experiments support the theory through distance approximation, spectrum preservation, graph classification using spectral information, and regression with graph convolutional networks. Together, these results connect a practical clustering method to a geometric account of what graph compression should retain.
icml-2023-a-gromov-wasserstein-geometric.tldr: A geometric theory connects graph-distance preservation to weighted kernel K-means for improved graph coarsening.

paragraphs: Biological sequence design often starts with a fixed collection of sequences and measured scores. Offline optimization uses that collection to propose sequences with better predicted scores. This paper develops bidirectional learning, where a forward mapping supports optimization and a backward mapping supplies a constraint.

An earlier approach builds its proxy using the neural tangent kernel of an infinitely wide network. The authors identify its inability to learn features and incorporate pretrained language models as obstacles. They instead attach a linear head to a pretrained biological language model and introduce a linearization scheme. This produces a closed-form loss while incorporating biophysical information represented by the pretrained model.

The method also learns how much weight to give each mapping, using an auxiliary model's weak supervision within a bilevel optimization framework. An extension, Adaptive-η, adapts learning rates and is compatible with gradient-based offline optimization algorithms. DNA and protein design experiments support the algorithm's effectiveness, linking pretrained sequence information with learned control over the optimization process.
icml-2023-bidirectional-learning-for-off.tldr: The method combines pretrained biological language models with learned bidirectional balancing and learning-rate adaptation for offline sequence design.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detectors help identify inputs that fall outside a classifier's familiar data distribution. A detector can flag an input without making its reasoning understandable. This paper addresses that interpretability problem by explaining detection decisions through learned high-level concepts.

The authors introduce two measures of how useful a concept set is. Detection completeness assesses whether the concepts contain enough information to explain the detector's decisions. Concept separability assesses how distinctly familiar and unfamiliar data are distributed in the concept representation. These measures address complementary questions: whether concepts account for the detector's behavior and whether they reveal differences between the two kinds of data.

An unsupervised learning framework seeks concept sets that score well on both properties. The authors demonstrate explanations for a variety of existing detectors and show how to identify concepts that contribute prominently to particular detection results. The contribution therefore extends beyond giving inputs a detection score: it provides a structured way to inspect what distinctions support that score.
icml-2023-concept-based-explanations-for.tldr: Learned high-level concepts explain out-of-distribution decisions using measures of decision coverage and distributional separation.

paragraphs: Many optimization guarantees rely on smoothness assumptions that do not cover important nonconvex machine learning problems. Applying algorithms designed around those assumptions can be suboptimal. This paper asks whether a broader class of functions can still be optimized with the efficiency established for smooth problems.

The authors introduce α-symmetric generalized smoothness, extending earlier definitions and covering important functions including high-order polynomials and exponentials. They establish basic properties and descent lemmas for this class. These lemmas provide the mathematical connection between taking an optimization step and making progress, supporting algorithm design under the broader condition.

A specially designed deterministic normalized gradient descent method achieves optimal iteration complexity O(ε⁻²). The authors also prove optimal sample complexity O(ε⁻³) for the SPIDER variance-reduction algorithm. These are different measures of computational effort: one counts iterations and the other samples. The results show that, for the generalized-smooth problems covered by the analysis, broadening the function class need not worsen these optimal complexity rates.
icml-2023-generalized-smooth-nonconvex-o.tldr: A broader generalized-smooth function class admits optimization algorithms with the same optimal complexity rates as smooth nonconvex problems.

paragraphs: Many graph neural networks use diffusion-inspired processing to move information through a graph. Repeated diffusion can produce oversmoothing, in which node representations become too alike. GREAD explores reaction–diffusion equations as a way to build graph neural networks that mitigate this problem.

Earlier reaction–diffusion approaches considered a limited selection of reaction equations. This work studies a broader range, covering popular forms and adding a specially designed reaction equation. The central design move is to expand the dynamics available to the network beyond diffusion alone. This makes the choice of reaction behavior an explicit part of constructing the graph model.

Across experiments involving nine datasets and 28 baselines, GREAD performs better in a majority of cases. Additional synthetic experiments show reduced oversmoothing and good performance across different homophily rates, which describe how similar connected nodes are. These findings support the usefulness of the reaction–diffusion approach across varied graph structures, while the reported majority-of-cases result preserves the distinction between broad empirical success and uniformly best performance.
icml-2023-gread-graph-neural-reaction-di.tldr: GREAD broadens reaction–diffusion graph neural networks and empirically mitigates oversmoothing while outperforming baselines in most evaluated cases.

paragraphs: Sparse coding represents a signal using a small number of elements from a learned dictionary. This paper examines what happens when the learned dictionary contains more elements than the dictionary that actually generated the data. That larger-dictionary setting becomes particularly challenging when observations contain noise.

The authors show that minimizing the standard dictionary-learning objective can fail to recover the true dictionary elements in this setting. Increasing the strength of the underlying signal does not necessarily resolve that failure. The result separates successful optimization of the usual objective from successful recovery of the structure that produced the observations.

Inspired by self-supervised learning, the authors introduce a masking objective. For a large class of data-generating processes, recovering the true dictionary becomes optimal as signal strength increases. This establishes a property of the objective, rather than claiming that every training run must recover the dictionary. Experiments across several parameter regimes support the theory and show better empirical performance than the standard reconstruction objective.
icml-2023-hiding-data-helps-on-the-benef.tldr: A masking objective can favor true dictionary recovery where standard noisy, over-realized sparse coding objectives can fail.

paragraphs: A transparent model can expose how it makes predictions while still behaving inconsistently with desired monotonic relationships. Monotonicity concerns whether model outputs respect specified directional relationships. This paper studies those requirements as a route to accountability and fairness in transparent machine learning models.

The authors distinguish three forms: individual monotonicity, weak pairwise monotonicity, and strong pairwise monotonicity. Their emphasis on pairwise requirements broadens the analysis beyond the individual monotonicity studied more commonly in earlier work. This matters because checking only one category of directional behavior does not address every category considered by the paper.

To combine these requirements with transparency, the authors propose monotonic groves of neural additive models. Their empirical examples show that monotonicity violations occur in practice and demonstrate transparent, accountable, and fair behavior for the proposed models. The findings position monotonicity as a concrete property to examine and enforce when managing model risk. The fairness conclusion is presented through those empirical examples and the paper's monotonicity-based approach.
icml-2023-how-to-address-monotonicity-fo.tldr: Monotonic groves of neural additive models address individual and pairwise monotonicity while preserving transparency.

paragraphs: This paper approaches adversarial examples as forensic evidence. The setting is a service provider that distributes model copies to customers, one of whom uses a copy to conduct attacks. The investigator seeks to trace the first compromised copy using available adversarial examples.

To make copies distinguishable through that evidence, the authors introduce random-mask watermarking. The mechanism is designed to differentiate adversarial examples associated with different model copies. Its role is to establish a traceable connection between an attack artifact and the distributed copy involved, supporting investigation after an attack has occurred.

The paper develops two tracing approaches for different evidence conditions. One uses the original, unmodified example alongside the adversarial example; the other works without access to that original input. Experiments spanning model architectures, attack methods, and datasets evaluate the framework's effectiveness. The contribution is an attribution capability within the model-distribution setting: it helps identify a compromised copy without requiring the tracing mechanism itself to prevent adversarial attacks.
icml-2023-identification-of-the-adversar.tldr: Random-mask watermarks enable forensic tracing of a compromised model copy from adversarial-example evidence.

paragraphs: Implicit video representations store video information in a neural model. Existing approaches emphasize network architecture and training the network's weights to represent a video. This paper explores whether useful video representations can instead be found inside a randomly initialized network by learning which parts to retain.

The approach learns multiple hierarchically organized supermasks for an image-wise video representation model while leaving its underlying weights unchanged. Each mask also receives its own trainable scale parameter. Compared with using the same fixed scale at every level, these adjustable scales enlarge the search space and allow exploration of more sparsity patterns.

Experiments on the UVG benchmark show that the selected random subnetworks achieve better reconstruction and visual quality than fully trained models with similar encoding sizes. The authors present this as evidence for strong lottery tickets in video representation models and provide a method for finding them. Learning remains essential to the approach: the optimized objects are the masks and their scales, rather than the original network weights.
icml-2023-is-overfitting-necessary-for-i.tldr: Learning hierarchical masks and scales within a fixed random network yields strong video representations without updating its underlying weights.

paragraphs: Denoising-based generative models have been successful for images and studied for continuous and categorical data. This paper identifies difficulties with some other data types, including counts and nonnegative measurements. Such data can contain many zeros, strongly uneven values, heavy tails, or substantial variation across observations.

The proposed alternative, learning to jump, builds training objectives through a forward process that thins counts. A neural network then supports a reverse process that thickens counts, iteratively refining generated samples. This pairs a count-based forward transformation with a corresponding generation procedure, giving the model a different foundation from learning to remove noise.

The authors examine when learning to jump is expected to perform similarly to denoising and when it is expected to work better. They recommend it for nonnegative training data with pronounced sparsity, skewness, heavy tails, or heterogeneity. The contribution is therefore a data-sensitive generative recipe: the stated advantage depends on the characteristics of the distribution being modeled, rather than applying uniformly to every type of data.
icml-2023-learning-to-jump-thinning-and-.tldr: Learning to jump uses count thinning and thickening to model data whose nonnegative, sparse, or uneven distributions can challenge denoising methods.

paragraphs: A language model that keeps learning from new data must adapt without losing useful knowledge from earlier training. Ordinary fine-tuning can overfit the latest distribution and cause catastrophic forgetting. This paper studies lifelong pretraining as a problem involving both training procedures and the capacity available to the model.

The authors identify additional capacity and appropriate regularization as key ingredients. Their Lifelong-MoE architecture grows by adding experts, with regularized pretraining accompanying that expansion. This gives the system new capacity as distributions change, extending approaches that keep the network architecture fixed throughout lifelong learning.

The reported results show that a limited number of additional experts enables continuing adaptation while retaining previous knowledge and keeping computation cost constant. Lifelong-MoE achieves better few-shot performance than existing lifelong-learning approaches and surpasses multitask learning on 19 downstream language-understanding tasks. These findings support expanding model capacity selectively: the model can gain parameters for new distributions without a corresponding increase in the reported computation cost.
icml-2023-lifelong-language-pretraining-.tldr: Lifelong-MoE adds regularized experts to adapt language models to changing data while preserving earlier knowledge at constant computation cost.

paragraphs: Mu²SLAM combines speech and text learning in a multilingual sequence-to-sequence model. Its pretraining uses unlabeled speech, unlabeled text, and supervised speech recognition, speech translation, and text translation data spanning more than 100 languages. The objective is to bring these languages and modalities into a shared model.

A quantized speech representation supplies targets for speech learning. Both speech and text use masked denoising on the decoder and masked language modeling on the encoder. Supervised tasks additionally help align representations across languages and between speech and text, connecting the different sources of training information.

On CoVoST speech translation, the model sets a new best result among models trained on public datasets, improving translation into English by 1.9 BLEU and from English by 1.1 BLEU. It matches the cited mSLAM speech-recognition performance on Voxpopuli despite a relatively weaker decoder. Text understanding also improves: XNLI gains exceed 6% over mSLAM, while results move closer to comparably sized mT5 models on XNLI and TydiQA.
icml-2023-mu-2-slam-multitask-multilingu.tldr: Mu²SLAM jointly learns speech and text across over 100 languages, improving speech translation and text understanding in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Neural recordings of complex behavior contain substantial noise, making behaviorally meaningful structure difficult to recover. Neural Latent Aligner uses repeated trials as a source of structure. Its unsupervised framework learns representations that agree across repetitions, emphasizing information that remains consistent from trial to trial.

Repetitions can differ in timing, so directly aligning them can obscure shared patterns. The authors introduce a fully differentiable time-warping model to handle temporal misalignment. Combining temporal alignment with representation learning lets the framework seek common neural information even when corresponding events occur at different times.

Applied to intracranial electrocorticography recordings of natural speech, NLA learns representations that support better behavioral decoding than the evaluated baselines, especially in lower-dimensional spaces. Behavioral coherence between aligned trials provides empirical validation of the time-warping component. The learned representations are also more consistent across trials, and visualizations reveal shared neural trajectories. These results support repeated-trial alignment as a useful constraint for extracting meaningful structure from complex, noisy recordings.
icml-2023-neural-latent-aligner-cross-tr.tldr: Neural Latent Aligner combines cross-trial consistency and learned time warping to extract behaviorally useful representations from neural recordings.

paragraphs: Federated Averaging trains a shared model through participating clients. Many earlier convergence analyses assume that every client participates or that participating clients can be sampled uniformly. Practical device availability depends on battery levels, connectivity, and participation-frequency requirements, which can instead create recurring patterns in who is available.

This paper develops a theoretical framework for analyzing FedAvg when client participation is cyclic. It covers several ways clients perform local optimization, including gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent, and shuffled stochastic gradient descent. The framework brings the participation pattern into the convergence analysis rather than treating uniform sampling as the default.

The analysis shows that cyclic participation can achieve a faster asymptotic convergence rate than vanilla FedAvg with uniform participation under suitable conditions. This is a conditional rate comparison, so it does not imply that every cyclic schedule improves training. Its significance is that recurring availability need not be treated only as a practical obstacle: the resulting structure can offer advantages that inform client-sampling protocol design.
icml-2023-on-the-convergence-of-federate.tldr: A convergence framework shows that cyclic client participation can accelerate FedAvg asymptotically under suitable conditions.

paragraphs: Personalized recommendation becomes costly when a system must learn separately for very many users. One way to share that effort is to identify groups whose members can receive the same recommendation with near-optimal results. This paper studies that grouping problem within contextual bandit learning.

The proposed algorithm, CLUB-HG, incorporates a game-theoretic approach into cluster inference. It reaches a Nash equilibrium at each inference step and discovers the underlying user clusters. The equilibrium condition supplies a notion of stability for the grouping process, connecting online recommendation with a structured way to infer which users belong together.

The authors provide regret analysis under a standard linear setting with stochastic noise. That analysis addresses the cost of learning while making recommendations within the stated model. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art algorithms. Together, the theory and experiments support clustering as a way to share learning across users while retaining the distinctions needed for useful personalization.
icml-2023-parallel-online-clustering-of-.tldr: CLUB-HG uses game-theoretic clustering to share contextual-bandit learning across users with similar recommendation needs.

paragraphs: Extreme multi-label classification selects relevant labels from a very large set of possibilities. Many methods concentrate on the meaning of an input's text. This paper argues that useful information also resides in label metadata and relationships among training instances, particularly in applications such as recommendations and product search.

PINA, or Predicted Instance Neighborhood Aggregation, is a data-augmentation method designed to use that side information. It extracts information from label descriptions or other metadata and from correlations between instances. This expands the evidence available to the classifier beyond treating each input and label as an isolated entry.

Experiments show consistent improvements across the evaluated extreme-classification tasks. PINA improves accuracy over standard XR-Transformers on five public benchmark datasets, including an approximately 5% gain on LF-AmazonTitles-1.3M, the largest dataset considered. The findings support incorporating relationships and metadata into the learning process. In this setting, improving prediction can come from making better use of the surrounding training information as well as the query text itself.
icml-2023-pina-leveraging-side-informati.tldr: PINA improves extreme multi-label classification by augmenting learning with label metadata and relationships among training instances.

paragraphs: Layout design requires arranging visual elements to satisfy a designer's intentions. Automating that work is useful only if the designer can communicate those intentions and influence the result. This paper targets the gap between generating layouts and providing controls that fit established design practices.

PLay is a conditional latent diffusion model that generates layouts in vector graphic space. Its conditioning comes from user-specified guidelines, a form designers already use to express layout intent. The approach therefore connects the generative model to a familiar input mechanism, making those guidelines part of the layout-generation problem itself.

The authors report better performance than prior methods across three datasets on measures including FID and FD-VG, as well as in a user test. They also present the method as enabling an interactive experience for professional layout design. The contribution combines two aspects of useful automation: producing stronger evaluated layouts and allowing users to steer generation through parameters grounded in their existing workflow.
icml-2023-play-parametrically-conditione.tldr: PLay generates vector layouts from designer-specified guidelines, combining interactive control with improved evaluated layout quality.

paragraphs: Mixup trains models on combinations of examples and their labels. This paper investigates its benefits through the features a classifier learns. The focus is on classes that have multiple useful cues, where learning one predictive cue can leave another available cue unused.

The theoretical analysis considers a nontrivial class of data distributions with two features per class and a two-layer convolutional network. Ordinary empirical risk minimization can learn only one feature for almost all classes. Under the analyzed setting, a particular Mixup variant succeeds in learning both features for every class, establishing a concrete difference in feature coverage.

Experiments on image benchmarks modified to contain multiple features support the relevance of these insights beyond the theoretical construction. The results offer an explanation for some of Mixup's observed benefits: its training procedure can encourage a model to acquire more of the available predictive information. The formal claim remains tied to the specified distributions, architecture, and Mixup instantiation, while the experiments provide evidence of broader practical relevance.
icml-2023-provably-learning-diverse-feat.tldr: For an analyzed two-feature setting, midpoint Mixup learns both class cues where ordinary training can learn only one.

paragraphs: Denoising diffusion models generate data by learning to reverse a process that transforms observations into noise. This paper interprets that process through image restoration. The connection allows ideas from restoration to guide both the training objective and the transformations used before reconstruction.

The authors use an alternative objective and forward processes that need not be diffusion processes. They incorporate prior knowledge into the loss through maximum a posteriori estimation, eliminating the need for the expensive sampling procedure associated with denoising diffusion models. They also introduce multiscale training, using the flexibility of the forward process to improve performance.

Experiments report improvements in quality and in the efficiency of both training and inference. The authors additionally demonstrate applications to inverse problems, extending the framework beyond generation alone. The central contribution is a restoration-based formulation that opens additional choices for how data are transformed and recovered. The experimental findings support those choices as useful design tools for generative modeling.
icml-2023-restoration-based-generative-m.tldr: An image-restoration view of generative modeling enables alternative objectives and forward processes that improve reported quality and efficiency.

paragraphs: Contextual pricing chooses prices using current customer information and past sales. A central difficulty is that the seller usually cannot observe a customer's valuation directly. The offered price reveals only partial information about that valuation, making it harder to learn a pricing rule from transactions.

CoxCP addresses this problem with an epoch-based algorithm using a Cox proportional hazards model for customer valuation. Its semiparametric formulation gives contextual effects a parametric form while leaving the baseline valuation nonparametric. This combines structure for learning the role of context with flexibility in the underlying valuation distribution.

For stochastic contexts, the authors establish a high-probability regret upper bound of roughly T^(2/3)d, suppressing logarithmic factors, where T is the horizon and d the context dimension. When the baseline is known, the bound improves to O(d log T) under additional assumptions. Experiments show better performance than existing semiparametric pricing algorithms when all compared algorithms' model assumptions hold, giving empirical support within that specified comparison setting.
icml-2023-semi-parametric-contextual-pri.tldr: CoxCP learns contextual prices from partially observed valuations using a semiparametric Cox model with conditional regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Using fewer observations might seem certain to hurt prediction, but this paper shows that downsampling can sometimes improve generalization in ridgeless linear regression. It presents downsampling as a counterpart to overparameterization, examining how the size of a data sketch changes prediction risk on unseen examples.

The analysis focuses on a proportional regime in which sketch size, sample size, and feature dimension are of comparable order. Within that setting, the authors investigate two out-of-sample risks and identify sketch sizes that minimize them. The optimally sketched estimator has more stable risk curves, removing peaks that appear for the full-sample estimator.

The paper also proposes an empirical procedure for choosing the sketch size, bringing the theoretical choice closer to practical use. Further analysis covers central limit theorems and misspecified models, and numerical studies strongly support the theory. The message is conditional but consequential: for the studied estimator and settings, retaining every observation need not yield the best generalization, and sketch size can be chosen for predictive performance.
icml-2023-sketched-ridgeless-linear-regr.tldr: Optimally chosen downsampling can improve ridgeless regression's prediction risk and remove peaks in its risk curves.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can produce networks that withstand tested attacks, but establishing a strong robustness certificate remains difficult. The paper identifies weaknesses in existing certification methods, particularly the barrier faced by linear-programming relaxations even when strengthened with mixed-integer and branch-and-bound techniques.

The proposed method applies a low-rank restriction to a semidefinite-programming relaxation, creating a nonconvex certification problem. Its aim is to retain the strength of more expensive semidefinite methods while optimizing a much smaller set of variables. The reported certificate strength is comparable to those methods, with variable counts comparable to weaker linear-programming approaches.

The authors also show how standard local optimization algorithms can achieve and certify global optimality for their formulation in polynomial time. That result concerns the proposed optimization formulation; the experiments separately assess how close its certificates come to exact network certification. Those experiments find that the method almost completely closes the gap for adversarially trained models, supporting low-rank nonconvex optimization as a practical route to stronger certificates.
icml-2023-tight-certification-of-adversa.tldr: A low-rank nonconvex semidefinite relaxation produces strong robustness certificates with substantially fewer optimization variables.

paragraphs: Understanding transformer expressivity means identifying which formal languages a transformer encoder can recognize. Connecting neural networks to formal computational systems gives a more precise way to discuss their capabilities. This paper narrows the gap between established lower and upper bounds on that recognition power.

Previous results connected transformer encoders to a type of counter machine and placed fixed-precision encoders within the complexity class uniform TC⁰. The authors link and strengthen these findings using a variant of first-order logic with counting quantifiers. This logical system becomes a common reference point for expressing what encoders can and cannot recognize.

Specifically, the logic provides an upper bound for fixed-precision transformer encoders and a lower bound for transformer encoders. The precision qualification matters because the two bounds are stated for differently qualified encoder settings. The result brings the field closer to an exact characterization without claiming that the remaining distinction has disappeared. Its contribution is a tighter formal description of recognition ability, rather than an empirical comparison of trained models.
icml-2023-tighter-bounds-on-the-expressi.tldr: A counting-based logical system tightens upper and lower bounds on the formal-language recognition power of transformer encoders.

paragraphs: Online learners must balance improving their choices against the cost of switching actions. Feedback determines how much they can learn without changing their behavior. This paper characterizes how both the quantity and type of observations affect the best achievable worst-case regret in that setting.

With ordinary bandit feedback plus a budget of extra observations, the authors identify a transition around T^(2/3) extra observations. Below that scale, regret remains of order T^(2/3), ignoring logarithmic factors. Above it, regret scales as T divided by the square root of the extra-observation budget, so additional feedback begins to improve the rate.

When the budget instead counts all observations, the optimal regret scales smoothly as T divided by the square root of that total budget, again up to logarithmic factors. A generic algorithmic framework achieves matching upper bounds in both settings. The results also distinguish feedback types: bandit feedback can remain optimal with a limited budget, but becomes insufficient for optimal regret when the available budget is relatively large.
icml-2023-understanding-the-role-of-feed.tldr: The paper precisely characterizes how observation budgets and feedback types control regret in online learning with switching costs.

paragraphs: Regression usually learns from exact numerical targets. In regression with interval targets, the supervision instead gives a range. This paper studies how to learn reliably from that weaker information, noting that adaptations of some related regression methods lack statistical consistency in this setting.

The authors first introduce a statistical model for the process that generates interval-target data and demonstrate its validity. They then analyze a simple selecting approach, which chooses one value from each interval and treats it as the training target. This makes explicit the consequences of converting a range into a single numerical label.

Their proposed limiting method trains by restricting predictions to the supplied intervals. They establish statistical consistency and derive an estimation-error bound, giving theoretical support under their formulation. Experiments across various datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The work therefore connects a model of how interval supervision arises with a learning objective that respects that supervision, providing both a theoretical foundation and empirical evidence for regression from ranges.
icml-2023-weakly-supervised-regression-w.tldr: A statistically consistent regression method learns from interval-valued supervision by limiting predictions to the supplied ranges.
